paragraphs.text: The Nanqiao in this brick’s name belongs to Menghai County [Nanqiao Tea Company](nanqiao-ruigong-brick:nanqiao-name), founded in February 2004, which kept the old name of the county around Mengzhe in southern Yunnan. It sells under the brand Che Fo Nan, and its teas have gone to Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia. Ruigong bricks travel that trade: at a [Malaysian tea fair](nanqiao-ruigong-brick:malaysian-tea-fair) in 2022, the exhibitor Quanyuxuan offered five of them together at stall 27, a ripe pressing from 2008.

This one is [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from Menghai leaf, made as a brick in 2009. Its leaf was [heaped in a damp pile](shou:wet-piling), warmed by its own microbes and turned to let air in. The method was meant to give in weeks what drinkers in Hong Kong and Guangdong once waited years for. At seventeen years it counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf still changes slowly with the air and moisture around it, so how it has been kept matters as much as the years.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
